Empirical Research Plan: “How Much of a Firm’s Market Value Is Tied to President Suharto?”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Chosen strategy: Repeated-event difference-in-differences (DiD) implemented as a stock-market event study.

Why this works
• The six well-defined rumor dates provide sharp, quasi-random information shocks about Suharto’s longevity.  
• Share-price data are intra-daily/daily, so market participants can react almost instantaneously, leaving little room for slow-moving confounders.  
• Cross-sectional heterogeneity in the Suharto Dependency Index lets us compare firms that are highly exposed to regime change with firms that are largely independent.  
• By estimating abnormal returns (ARs) around each rumor and comparing ARs across dependency groups, we difference out both market-wide news and firm fixed effects, satisfying the spirit of DiD.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the group’s Castle Suharto Dependency Index ≥ 3 (moderate to very high reliance). We can also estimate with the continuous 1–5 score.

Control group  
All publicly listed firms in the sample with Dependency Index ≤ 2 (low or none).

Treatment timing / event dates  
Six rumor episodes between 1995 and 1997 (dates supplied in the chronology). For each episode we use:

• Event day 0: first trading day the rumor hits the wires.  
• Estimation window: −130 to −10 trading days (to estimate factor model betas).  
• Event window: [0, +2] trading days for baseline; robustness windows [−1,+1] and [0,+5].

No running variable is required because we do not use RDD.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel counterfactual trends  
Absent the health rumor, abnormal returns of treated and control firms would have behaved similarly during the event window. Plausible because windows are only a few days long and Indonesia’s overall macro backdrop is common to all listed firms.

A2. Exogenous timing of rumors  
Health-scare rumors are largely outside the control of firms and investors; hence the treatment shock is as-good-as-random.

A3. No differential anticipation  
Markets do not systematically anticipate the exact day rumors emerge. Short windows help.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA)  
One firm’s exposure does not alter another firm’s returns in the three-day window, conditional on market return controls.

A5. Constant group classification  
The Dependency Index is measured in 1995 and does not change during 1995-97 for large conglomerates; hence no composition changes.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Other macro news (e.g., Asian financial jitters) coinciding with rumor days  
• Mitigation: (i) subtract market-model abnormal returns using JSX index; (ii) include sector*event fixed effects; (iii) perform placebo tests on pseudo-event dates.

T2. Mis-measurement of political ties  
• Mitigation: (i) Use alternative binary classifications from analysts; (ii) run specifications with continuous score; (iii) instrument score with “family tie” dummies (child-controlled firms) as a robustness exercise.

T3. Liquidity differences (connected firms may be larger & more liquid)  
• Mitigation: Control for log market cap, pre-event turnover, and add stock-specific volatility in cross-sectional regression; also run equal- and value-weighted estimations.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # DiD regressions
library(PerformanceAnalytics)  # abnormal returns
library(lubridate)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
# -------------------------------------------------
prices  <- fread("daily_prices.csv")      # firm_id, date, price
funds   <- fread("accounting_1995.csv")   # firm_id, assets, debt, etc.
deps    <- fread("dependency_index.csv")  # firm_id, dep_score
events  <- fread("suharto_rumor_dates.csv") # event_id, event_date

# Merge
dt <- merge(prices, deps, by="firm_id")
dt <- merge(dt, funds, by="firm_id")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------------
# daily returns
setorder(dt, firm_id, date)
dt[, ret := (price / shift(price) - 1), by = firm_id]

# market return
market <- dt[, .(mkt_ret = weighted.mean(ret, w = assets, na.rm = TRUE)), by = date]
dt <- merge(dt, market, by = "date")

# abnormal return via simple market model
dt[, ar := ret - mkt_ret]

# treatment indicator
dt[, treat := as.integer(dep_score >= 3)]

# Event windows
win <- 2   # +2 days
ew  <- dt[, .(firm_id, date)]
for(i in 1:nrow(events)){
  e0 <- events$event_date[i]
  ew[, paste0("event_",i) := between(date, e0, e0 + win)]
}
# Stack to long event format
long <- melt(ew, id.vars = c("firm_id","date"), variable.name = "event", 
             value.name = "in_window")[in_window == TRUE]
long[, event_id := as.integer(gsub("event_","",event))]
long <- merge(long, dt, by = c("firm_id","date"))

# Cumulative abnormal return per event per firm
car <- long[, .(CAR = sum(ar, na.rm=TRUE)), by = .(firm_id, event_id, treat, dep_score,
                                                   assets, industry = ISIC)]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Regression
# -------------------------------------------------
# DiD with event fixed effects
m1 <- feols(CAR ~ treat | event_id + industry, data = car, cluster = "firm_id")
summary(m1)

# Continuous intensity
m2 <- feols(CAR ~ dep_score | event_id + industry, data = car, cluster = "firm_id")
summary(m2)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Placebo (shift events by +20 trading days)
events[, placebo := event_date + 20]
# repeat window construction & regression; compare coefficients
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Prediction: Rumors of Suharto’s ill-health will produce negative abnormal returns for highly connected firms relative to independent firms. Magnitude: −2 % to −4 % cumulative abnormal return over three days for treated firms; control firms close to zero.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel short-run trends ➔ 0.8  
C2: Exogenous treatment timing ➔ 1.0  
C3: No spillovers/SUTVA ➔ 0.8  
C4: Stable composition of groups ➔ 1.0  
C5: No differential anticipation ➔ 0.7  

Total (out of 5) = 4.3 – overall credible, but still requires placebo and pre-trend diagnostics.
